# IEA "Electricity 2026" — Executive summary

IEA (2026), *Electricity 2026*, IEA, Paris.

## Key figures
- Global electricity demand forecast to grow at an average annual rate of 3.6% over 2026–2030 (industry, EVs, air conditioning, data centres). 2025: +3% y/y; 2024: +4.4%.
- For the first time in three decades (excluding crisis periods), global electricity demand outpaced economic growth in 2024.
- Emerging economies account for nearly 80% of additional electricity consumption through 2030. China: close to 50% of the increase; over the next five years China adds demand equivalent to the EU's total electricity consumption today, growing 4.9% annually.
- Advanced economies: ~20% of global demand growth in 2025 (up from 17% in 2024). US demand +2.1% in 2025, ~2% annually through 2030, with around half of the total increase driven by data centres.
- Renewables overtake coal: renewable output in 2025 virtually matched coal-fired generation. Renewable output forecast to grow ~1,000 TWh annually through 2030 (solar PV alone >600 TWh); +8% per year.
- Renewables and nuclear together expected to account for around half of global electricity generation by 2030.
- Nuclear generation set a new record in 2025; China alone ~40% of the global increase through 2030.
- Coal: broadly flat in 2025; declines in India and China, increases in the US. Coal remains the single largest source of electricity in 2030 (near its 2021 level).
- Gas-fired generation grows 2.6% per year through 2030.
- Solar PV + wind share of global generation rises from 17% today to 27% by 2030.
- >2,500 GW of projects (renewables, storage, large loads incl. data centres) stalled in grid connection queues worldwide. Annual grid investment must increase ~50% by 2030 from today's USD 400 billion.
- Grid-enhancing measures could unlock 1,200–1,600 GW of queued projects (750–900 GW via non-firm connections; 450–700 GW via grid-enhancing technologies).
- Global power sector emissions flat in 2025, forecast to plateau over 2026–2030. Electricity generation produces ~13,900 Mt CO2 annually; CO2 intensity down 14% vs. a decade earlier.
